result.title: AGPAT2 Inflammatory Metabolic Reprogramming Mediates Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-associated Myocarditis via LPAR5-pyroptosis Axis
result.authorString: Chen Y, Shen Y, ZHANG H, Wang X, Xu Y, Zhang J, He X, Han M, Cheng L, Ge J.
result.abstractText:
Objectives:

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), especially programmed cell death protein-1 (PD1) inhibitors, are effective onco-therapeutic agents. However, ICI-associated myocarditis (ICIAM) greatly limits their clinical utility. Imbalance between 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferases (AGPAT2) and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) induced by inflammatory metabolic reprogramming (IMRP) might cause cardiovascular injury. This study aims to explore the link between AGPAT2 pathway and ICIAM as well as identifies diagnosis and treatment targets of ICIAM.

Methods:

ICIAM model was established by injecting anti-PD1 (αPD1) in wild-type (WT) and AGPAT2 heterozygous knockout (AGPAT2+/-) mice. The pathogenic and regulating mechanisms of AGPAT2-LPA and its downstream signaling were examined in vitro and in vivo. A tumor-patient cohort was enrolled to observe the association between serum LPA and risk of ICIAM.

Results:

In the αPD1-induced ICIAM model, myocardial IMRP occurred due to upstream immunity disorder, leading to downstream AGPAT2 degradation via lysosomal pathway and subsequent LPA accumulation. Knockout of AGPAT2 gene also promoted LPA accumulation. The accumulated LPA, by binding to its dominant receptor subtype 5 (LPAR5), triggered pyroptotic myocardial damage and resultant ICIAM. LPAR5 knockdown with siRNA or inhibition with TCLPA5-4 played the most significant rescue effect on myocardial pyroptosis, while stimulating LPAR5 with overdose LPA significantly increased myocardial pyroptosis. In ICI-treated patients, elevated serum LPA was associated with increased risk of ICIAM.

Conclusions:

IMRP-triggered dysfunction of AGPAT2-LPA-LPAR5-pyroptosis axis is involved in pathogenesis of ICIAM. Several elements in this axis may be the promising targets in diagnosis (LPA as a biomarker) and treatment (LPA or LPAR5 as therapeutics) of ICIAM.

result.title: Accessibility-guided targeting of NRF2-responsive long noncoding RNA NMRAL2P alters a distinct gene expression program and reduces non-small cell lung cancer proliferation
result.authorString: Bucknor JA, Bowman BM, Stein SL, Weidmann CA.
result.abstractText: Aberrant activation of the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 promotes non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) survival and therapy resistance, but downstream effectors beyond redox regulation remain incompletely defined. Transcriptome profiling of lung and NSCLC cells identified the pseudogene-derived long noncoding RNA LOC344887/NMRAL2P as consistently associated with NRF2 activity. The NMRAL2P locus produces three predominant, nuclear-localized isoforms whose expression depends on NRF2 across normal lung, lung adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous carcinoma cells. In-cell SHAPE-MaP identified accessible regions within NMRAL2P transcripts, guiding antisense gapmer design. NMRAL2P depletion inhibited NSCLC cell proliferation and increased sensitivity to cisplatin. Transcriptome analysis revealed that NMRAL2P depletion altered a restricted gene expression program involving cell adhesion and MAPK signaling, with responses distinct from those observed following NRF2 depletion. Core NRF2 antioxidant target genes were largely unaffected by NMRAL2P depletion. These findings support a model in which NRF2 induces NMRAL2P to sustain a distinct gene expression program that contributes to NSCLC proliferation and survival. NMRAL2P represents an RNA effector downstream of NRF2 that links oncogenic NRF2 activity to cellular functions beyond canonical antioxidant responses, providing a potential point of intervention in NRF2-active lung cancers and motivating further investigation of the mechanisms connecting this nuclear RNA to signaling pathways.

result.title: Diabetes-associated lung physiology shapes Klebsiella pneumoniae infection dynamics
result.authorString: Gunter K, Todd K, Bowen JM, Le MT, Wilson K, Holmes CL, Hullahalli K, Tilston-Lunel NL, Vornhagen J.
result.abstractText: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with increased susceptibility to bacterial pneumonia, yet the mechanisms by which diabetic host physiology influences pathogen establishment remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated how diabetes-associated changes in the lung environment influence  Klebsiella pneumoniae infection using leptin receptor-deficient (  db/db ) mice. Following acute lung infection,  db/db mice exhibited increased bacterial burdens compared to nondiabetic controls, despite mounting a robust inflammatory cytokine response. Elevated pulmonary vascular endothelial growth factor concentrations were accompanied by alterations in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metabolite profile, including enrichment of several amino acids and related metabolites. Consistent with increased nutrient availability,  K. pneumoniae exhibited enhanced growth in BALF from  db/db mice, and a glutamate-auxotrophic mutant demonstrated improved fitness during pulmonary infection. Using a barcoded  K. pneumoniae library, we found that  db/db mice supported significantly larger initial founding populations, leading to increased bacterial burden in the lungs. Increased founding populations were also observed in the liver and coincided with proportionally wider infection bottlenecks in the lung. Together, these findings demonstrate that diabetes-associated changes in lung physiology coincide with increased nutrient availability and reduced restrictions on bacterial establishment, highlighting bacterial founding population size as a distinct determinant of pneumonia susceptibility in T2DM.

result.title: High-Throughput Screen of Advanced Repurposing Library Identifies Compounds Active Against Acute and Chronic Stages of Toxoplasma gondii
result.authorString: Uddin T, McNamara CW, Chatterjee AK, Sibley LD.
result.abstractText: Toxoplasma gondii, a pathogen with a global burden impacting millions, has the capability to interconvert between the actively replicating tachyzoite form into a semidormant bradyzoite for, complicating treatment. Here, we utilized an advanced high throughput screen (HTS) to identify repurposing candidates from the ReFRAME library, which consolidates 14,095 molecules from three major databases, including FDA approved and late-stage clinical leads. To facilitate screening, the permissive cyst-forming Tg68 strain was genetically engineered to express nano luciferase under the pBAG1 promoter to track bradyzoite growth, and firefly luciferase under the pTub1 promoter to monitor tachyzoite growth. HTS in 384 well format identified 160 compounds that exhibited > 80% inhibition at 10 micromolar of both tachyzoites and bradyzoites. By cross referencing against a publicly available HEK293T cytotoxicity dataset, we filtered out 61 compounds based on half-maximal cytotoxicity (CC50) less < 5 micromolar, leaving 99 for further evaluation. From this set, 15 top hits were identified based on potency and the selectivity index (CC50:EC50; SI > 20) against HepG2. The top hits were profiled using in vitro growth assays for tachyzoites, bradyzoites, and ex vivo liberated and intact cysts. Marizomib, monensin, narasin, and LY2090314 showed the strongest inhibition following 24 h treatment of intact cysts. When tested in combination with clinical compounds atovaquone and pyrimethamine, the top hits were predominantly additive. Additionally, they were evaluated for their potential for developing resistance using a minimum inoculum of resistance (MIR) assay. Six of nine compounds tested in MIR assays yielded no detectable parasites over 30 days. In contrast, LY2090314 resistant populations exhibited 26 to 29-fold resistance and carried a TgGSK3 L53V mutation, identifying a candidate resistance determinant. Collectively, our findings identify compounds with activity against tachyzoites and bradyzoites and with low propensity for resistance, as starting points for mechanistic investigation and further evaluation of in vivo efficacy and host-toxicity liabilities.

result.title: Optimizing Avian Influenza Viral RNA Enrichment from Water: A Comparison of Concentration Methods for Low-Volume Samples
result.authorString: Neumann Heise J, Holzer C, Stange C, Thiem A, Perlas A, Urban L, Harder TC, Breuer L, Knauf S, Globig A.
result.abstractText: Feed-baited water bins may provide a complementary approach for avian influenza virus (AIV) surveillance in wild waterbird populations. In a previous study, water from these bins was sampled using swabs after exposure to visiting birds, but the low sample volume limited the detection and subsequent characterization of AIV RNA (F. I. Rondi, J. Neumann-Heise, T. Harder, V. Allendorf, K. Depner, T. Homeier-Bachmann, L. Breuer, S. Knauf, S. Dreyer, and A. Globig, One Health 23:101548, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.onehlt.2026.101548). Here, we compared five sample-processing methods for improving AIV RNA detection in small (40-mL) water samples (tap and brackish water) spiked with an AIV of the H4N6 subtype under simulated field conditions: swab sampling, polyethylene glycol precipitation, activated carbon capture, combined activated carbon capture and polyethylene glycol precipitation (AC/PEG), and electronegative membrane adsorption (EM). AC/PEG and EM showed the strongest overall performance based on RT-qPCR results, although their relative performance varied across experimental conditions. The qPCR-derived viral signal was generally higher in tap water than in brackish water, whereas wheat presence was associated with a lower signal, particularly for swab sampling. Subsequent testing was conducted to ascertain the most effective storage conditions with regard to temperature and duration. During storage, AIV RNA detection remained relatively stable at minus 20 degrees Celsius for up to four weeks, with only minor increases in mean Ct values in both water matrices. Greater increases were observed at room temperature and 4 degrees Celsius, with significantly higher Ct values at both temperatures than at minus 20 degrees Celsius in both water matrices at Weeks 2 and 4 (p < 0.05). These findings support the potential of AC/PEG and EM to facilitate the recovery, detection and subsequent characterization of AIV from low-volume water samples by improving viral RNA detection using RT-qPCR. Given its overall performance and lower cost compared with EM, AC/PEG may represent a practical option for field-based surveillance. Regarding storage, minus 20 degrees Celsius provided the best conditions for maintaining AIV RNA detection, with relatively stable results for up to four weeks.

result.title: Scalable recorders of cellular calcium dynamics and molecular interactions across time
result.abstractText: Cellular processes are mediated by dynamic biochemical events in their native context, including changes in intracellular ion concentrations and transient interactions between molecules. Studying these processes across large cell populations requires recording their dynamics across time in single cells, simultaneously and at scale. Here, we introduce split-1POK, a split protein tape monomer whose two halves reconstitute when the domains fused to them interact. The reconstituted monomer is incorporated into the protein tape as it elongates across time in live cells, enabling scalable, spatiotemporally resolved endpoint readout under conventional light microscopy. Split-1POK provides a programmable scaffold for new recorders in the CytoSense family, our previously introduced framework (ref. 1) in which the same cytosol-localized monomer senses cellular activity and writes it along protein tape recorders. Unlike transcription-based activity recorders, which encode the signal through new gene expression, CytoSense recorders act on monomers post-synthesis, so the activity signal is sensed and written directly in the cytosol without passing through transcription- or translation-associated cascades. Fusing calmodulin and its binding peptide to split-1POK, we built TCaMP (Tape monomer-CalModulin-Peptide), a genetically encoded calcium recorder (GECR) that measures calcium dynamics on a single, analog intensity scale along a continuous time axis, providing quantitative comparison of calcium levels over time within the same cell. In cultured human cells, TCaMP records transient calcium dynamics from transmembrane entry, receptor activation, and intracellular store release, detecting stimulations as brief as ten minutes. With hour-scale kinetics over days, TCaMP complements fluorescent calcium indicators by trading sub-second temporal resolution for scalable, long-term recording. Fusing conditional dimerization pairs to split-1POK yields recorders of molecular interaction histories in response to external stimuli. Split-1POK thus brings scalable, spatiotemporally resolved recording to intracellular calcium dynamics and molecular interactions across time.
